doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Miles Davis as a young man and the Grammy request
summary: Carter found Miles quiet and lyrical, let him stay in his house, and later accepted a Grammy for him.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: Again, one of these, you know, useless questions that . . . open-ended, but what are your recollections of Miles at this period when he first joined you? Musically, what did you hear in him that may have been different from other musicians at the time?

Well, I just heard something different. I can’t tell you what, you know, but I heard something different than . . . I can’t explain what I heard. He had that sort of lyrical thing. He didn’t do a lot of soloing in my group, and there was no way of knowing or being able to foretell what he was going to become.
Well, again, I hate to try and draw out personal observations. You obviously didn’t know him that well at the time.
Not at all.
But did you get an impression of him? Was he quiet?
He was very quiet. Oh yes, he was very quiet, almost to say retiring, you know. No, he was very nice young man, you know. [unclear] he was well-bred, and he was a lovely man, you know.
In his book, his autobiography, which came out a couple of years ago, he mentions that he stayed in your home in Los Angeles. Is that true?
Yes. Yes.
Did he have no other place to go or you were just . . .

Well, I don’t know. You know, he was a stranger here, and I had a house here, and there was nobody in it but me and the houseboy [laughs], you know, so . . . I shouldn’t say “the houseboy,” but someone that took care of the house and helped me, you know. I don’t like the term houseboy, really.
Well, there’s another word for it; I can’t think of it at the moment, but the . . .
If it was a big house and a big family, you’d probably call it major domo or something.
Right. [laughs]
Is that what you’re thinking?
Or the housekeeper or the something, whatever.
Yeah, yeah. But he was really a friend, you know. But [unclear] not much I can tell you about Miles, of that period.
How about of another period, a later period?
Well, we weren’t part of each other’s activities at a later period. He went on to New York, and that was it. Everybody knows what happened after that, much more than I do.
Were you in touch with him, ever, after . . .
No. No.
Not a single time.
No, no reason to be. No.
I believe when he was once given an award—I’ve forgot what award it was—you . . .
The Grammy Award.
Was it a Grammy?
Yeah.
And did he personally ask you if you would accept it for him?
Yeah, he called and asked if I would accept for him. That’s right.
So he must have remembered . . . had some feeling for your association.
Well, he remembered and knew that I was here, you know.
